assignments.title: Primary Source Report: The Rights of Man and Robespierre
assignments.html:
PRIMARY SOURCE REPORT
The Rights of Man and Robespierre
The French Revolution
16 points · text entry
★ ✦ ★
Before you start

Finish both lessons and read both sources first. Your notes from each page are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the page, so open it before you write. Then write your answers and submit them in this assignment.

QUESTIONS
1. The National Assembly approved the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in August 1789. Robespierre gave his speech on political morality to the Convention in 1794. For each document, say who is speaking, who the audience is, and what had happened in France just before. How might those differences change what each document can teach us?
2. Choose one article of the Declaration. Quote it in a few words, then explain in your own words what it promises. Then name one group of people that the lesson “1789: The Bastille and the Rights of Man” shows was left out or only slowly included, and say what that shows about the gap between the words and the law.
3. Robespierre says that virtue is the spirit of a republic and that terror is a tool to defend it. Compare this with what the Declaration says about liberty and about the law applying equally to all. Which promise of the Declaration is most at risk under Robespierre's argument, and why? Use evidence from both documents.
4. Robespierre believed he was defending a pure cause against corrupt enemies. Using his speech and the lesson “Terror and Thermidor: Robespierre and the Republic of Virtue”, explain how a leader's sincere belief could still lead a government to the Terror. Then say one thing his speech cannot tell us about how the Terror felt to the people who lived through it.
GRADING RUBRIC (16 pts)
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1)
Understanding of the material
4 pts		 Reads both sources accurately and draws on specific details from each, along with what the week's lessons taught. Reads both sources accurately but uses few specific details, or leans on only one. Shows partial understanding of one or both sources, with some errors or vague claims. Misreads the sources or does not refer to them.
Quality of reasoning
4 pts		 Connects each claim to evidence and compares the sources with care. Explains why the speaker, the audience, and the moment matter. Supports most claims with evidence. The comparison is sound but not fully developed. States conclusions with little support, or describes the sources without comparing them. Offers opinions without evidence from the sources.
Clarity and precision of expression
4 pts		 Writes in clear, well-organized sentences. Quotations are short, accurate, and introduced. Writing is clear with minor lapses in organization or precision. Writing is often unclear or disorganized, and quotations are unclear or misplaced. Writing is too unclear to follow.
Intellectual honesty
4 pts		 Names the limits of what each source can show and says what remains uncertain without overclaiming. Acknowledges at least one limit of the evidence. Mentions limits only in passing, or claims more than the sources allow. Treats each source as complete and beyond question.
Total:
16 pts total
SUBMISSION

Answer all four questions in complete sentences. Submit your answers in the text box on the Canvas assignment page. Aim for one solid paragraph for each question. You do not need an outside source. Your teacher will read your work and return a rubric score with a short comment.

quizzes.title: Module Intro: The French Revolution
quizzes.description:
MODULE INTRO
The French Revolution
2 questions · survey · one attempt
★ ✦ ★
Essential question for this week
How did a dispute over politics and money become a revolution, and why did the revolution turn to terror?
Instructions

Welcome to The French Revolution. This short check-in is not graded. Your answers help your teacher see where each student is starting, so answer honestly.

What you will be able to do

1789: The Bastille and the Rights of Man

  • Explain how the fall of the Bastille turned a political dispute into a revolution.
  • Summarize the main changes the National Assembly made between 1789 and 1791.
  • Identify the tensions in the Declaration of the Rights of Man and in the Constitution of 1791.

Terror and Thermidor: Robespierre and the Republic of Virtue

  • Explain how war and fear pushed the Revolution toward the Reign of Terror.
  • Describe what Robespierre meant by a Republic of Virtue and why his colleagues turned against him.
  • Evaluate how ideas, fear, and chance each contributed to the Terror.

discussions.title: Discussion: Could the Revolution Have Stopped in 1791?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Could the Revolution Have Stopped in 1791?
The French Revolution
10 points · threaded discussion
★ ✦ ★
Before you start

Finish both lessons first. Your notes from each lesson are kept in My Notebook, the button inside the lesson, so open it before you post. Then post your answer here and reply to one classmate.

DISCUSSION PROMPT

By September 1791 France had a Declaration of Rights, equality before the law, and a constitution that made the king a limited monarch. Yet within two years the king was dead and the Terror had begun. The lessons show a king who did not trust the settlement, deputies who did not trust the king, a Church divided by the oath, and a war that began in 1792.

Take a position. Could the Revolution have stopped in 1791? Support your position with at least two specific details from the lessons, and include one detail that points the other way. Explain why you weigh the evidence as you do.

Aim for about 150 to 200 words.

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a detail from the lessons that they did not use. If not, explain respectfully where it falls short, and point to a detail from the lessons that supports your view.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
Criteria Substantive (full credit) Thin (partial credit) Missing (no credit)
Claim and evidence
5 pts		 Takes a clear position, supports it with at least two specific details from the lessons, and deals fairly with a detail that points the other way. Takes a position but gives only one detail, or stays general, or ignores the opposing detail. No post, or no clear position.
Response to a classmate
5 pts		 Answers a specific point in a classmate's post and either strengthens it with a new detail or explains politely where it falls short. Replies in general terms, such as agreeing or disagreeing without a detail from the lessons. No reply.
10 pts total
